newsitem.title: CANADA: On the Internet the future is nigh.
newsitem.headline: On the Internet the future is nigh.

text.p: TORONTO (REUTER) - The Internet is supposed to be the cool place to hang out, but for many of us it's been more sizzle than substance.

The good news is that things will get better as the world's interconnection of computers matures and allows compelling capabilities -- such as chat rooms that will evolve into face-to-face meetings and simple graphics that will give way to multi-dimensional animations.

The bad news, however, is that the process will take time, frustrating browsers and driving up costs and complexity for individuals, organisations and companies looking to post sites on the World Wide Web.
One of the bigger problems now is the difficulty in predicting how many people are actually on the Internet and how that number will grow.
Making predictions about the Web is always a dangerous game; especially when it is remembered that seemingly no one predicted its rise in the first place.

But of the forecasters, International Data Corp. has predicted the Internet's population would rise to 200 million by 2000 from 40 million now while Forrester Research saw the Web's population topping 100 million by 1999.
This prediction of future growth comes amid constant criticism that the Web today is far from perfect.

Michael West, an Internet analyst at the Gartner Group, sees the current environment as "unstable" where computing standards are being developed haphazardly. This used to be okay when academics dominated the Internet, but it has proved difficult for individuals and corporations.
Today, Internet software products need to be tested across a variety of competing platforms and too often many have not been ready for prime time.
"We are doing free beta testing for them," noted West at a recent Gartner Group conference. "It's a very interesting era we are in."
As well, unlike the fast food business, no safe economic "model" has emerged for those entrepreneurs on the Internet.
"We have no certain business model," said West. "We haven't got the McDonald's franchise model where you know you can make money if you just work hard."
But not to worry, this is not about to stop the unstoppable, the amazing explosion of the Internet into the all pervasive thing it is supposed to become.

West said the lack of standards on the Internet, including standards for safe financial transactions, would continue to drive up Internet publishing costs. He said it would be many years before users feel safe paying for goods over the Net.
"Through 1999, the instability, immaturity and inadequacy of Internet standards will drive the cost and complexity of developing and maintaining applications," he said.
But he maintained that while many Web publishers will drop off because of costs and other problems, many will also persevere.

Because of this, he expected the "freebie" Internet products (though we assumed this would not include Microsoft's Internet Explorer) would recede into the background as customers demand more sophisticated and robust products that do the job as advertised.

Corporate Web sites will become more exciting and relevant to keep customers coming back. Those one dimensional graphics will not do it anymore and companies will move to a new echelon of three-dimensional imagery and animations.

As well, static newsgroups and chat areas will develop into full fledged Web "conferencing" complete with both audio and visual capabilities. That's means instead of just exchanging notes, you would be able to see and hear the person you have just met from a far flung corner of the globe.
So as the Web matures perhaps we will also. For the first time we may soon have to get all dressed up just to chat.
--Russell Blinch (416) 941-8103, or e-mail: russell.blinch@reuters.com
